content: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a lung infection that develops outside of hospital settings. It is the most prevalent type of pneumonia and a significant cause of illness and death. Symptoms often include difficulty breathing, fever, chest pain, and coughing. CAP occurs when the alveoli, the small air sacs in the lungs, fill with fluid, impairing their function. The condition can be caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites. Diagnosis is often based on clinical symptoms and physical examination, but additional tests such as chest x-rays, sputum analysis, and other laboratory studies are frequently employed. Treatment primarily involves antibiotics, and certain forms of CAP can be prevented through vaccination. Sir William Osler, often referred to as the Father of Modern Medicine, recognized the severe impact of pneumonia, famously calling it the Captain of the Men of Death in 1918. However, advancements in the 20th century, including the development of penicillin, other antibiotics, modern surgical techniques, and intensive care, significantly reduced pneumonia-related mortality in developed countries. The introduction of vaccines, such as the Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine in 1988 and the Streptococcus pneumoniae vaccine for adults in 1977 and for children in 2000, led to a marked decline in cases. Pathogens can enter the lungs through aspiration, circulation, local spread, traumatic inoculation, or medical interventions. Impaired immunity or an inability to filter out pathogens increases the risk of developing pneumonia. The specific cause of CAP varies depending on factors such as age, immune status, geographic location, and underlying health conditions. CAP can be caused by a range of pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi. The most common cause in adult outpatients and inpatients is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Patients in intensive care units are more likely to have infections caused by aggressive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus or Gram-negative bacilli. In neonates, Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the leading cause of pneumonia during the first week of life. Children and elderly individuals are more susceptible to viral infections and atypical bacterial pneumonias caused by organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Legionella species. It is important to differentiate CAP from other conditions that can present with similar symptoms, such as interstitial lung disease, congestive heart failure (CHF), cancer, and pulmonary embolism. Pneumonia is the leading cause of death in children under five years of age worldwide, with higher mortality rates in developing countries. Both children and the elderly are at increased risk of complications from pneumonia. Despite appropriate antibiotic treatment, complications such as sepsis, respiratory failure, pleural effusion, and empyema can occur, particularly in bacterial pneumonia. Most bacterial pneumonias resolve within one to two weeks with proper treatment, while viral pneumonias may take longer, and mycoplasmal pneumonia can take four to six weeks to fully resolve. The prognosis depends on the severity of the illness at the time of diagnosis. The CURB-65 score is a clinical tool used to predict mortality in CAP and assess disease severity. Another tool, the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI), helps estimate the likelihood of morbidity and mortality in CAP patients. Common symptoms of CAP include cough, fever, and difficulty breathing. Patients often report a history of close contact with others who have similar symptoms. Severe cases may present with cyanosis (bluish skin), confusion, or respiratory distress, requiring immediate medical attention. Abnormal lung findings, such as crackles (rales), increased loudness of whispered speech (whispered pectoriloquy), or reduced breath sounds, may indicate lung consolidation. Palpation and percussion of the chest can help localize areas of consolidation, and increased tactile fremitus (vibration felt on the chest during speech) may also be noted. Laboratory findings, such as leukocytosis, can support the diagnosis of bacterial pneumonia and help assess the patient’s condition. Sputum samples should be collected for Gram staining and culture to identify the causative pathogen. Additional tests, such as urine antigen tests, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin levels, may also be useful. Chest x-rays are a key diagnostic tool for pneumonia, often revealing areas of lung consolidation as white opacities. However, early-stage pneumonia or infections in less visible lung regions may not appear on x-rays. In cases where x-rays are inconclusive, chest CT scans can provide more detailed imaging, showing findings such as lobar consolidation, ground-glass opacities, pleural effusion, lymphadenopathy, or a tree-in-bud pattern. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) can help identify uncommon pathogens and differentiate CAP from non-infectious causes of lung disease. Treatment of CAP involves the use of appropriate antibiotics and management of complications. Empiric therapy is often initiated before culture results are available and is tailored based on disease severity, as determined by tools like the PSI and CURB-65 score. Empiric regimens typically cover both typical and atypical bacterial pathogens. Once culture results are obtained, therapy can be adjusted to target the specific pathogen.
